newsitem.title: PERU: American nations to pledge democratic commitment.
newsitem.headline: American nations to pledge democratic commitment.

text.p: The 34 nations of the Organisation of American States (OAS) nations will sign a joint pledge to uphold democracy and human rights throughout the continent at their 27th annual assembly starting on Sunday.

"The promotion and consolidation of democracy and the respect for human rights are the fundamental elements for inter-American cooperation and solidarity," said a preliminary copy of the Lima Declaration to be signed at the end of the five-day conference.

The six-point declaration, obtained by Reuters, also promised to step up efforts "to combat and eradicate terrorism, corruption, the illicit trafficking of narcotics and of arms, munitions and explosives."
It contained few specifics, however, on how to tackle these traditional problems, which have plagued Latin America and the Caribbean for decades.
And the largely predictable declaration made no reference to the blemished human rights and democracy records of some member nations.

Host country Peru, for example, is under fire for alleged continued abuses in its 17-year war on leftist guerrillas, and the widely perceived steam-rollering of independent democratic institutions by an authoritarian government.

The government-controlled Congress unleashed a furore this week when it voted to dismiss three members of Peru's highest constitutional court who were blocking a possible third election bid by President Alberto Fujimori in 2000.
OAS Secretary-General Cesar Gaviria refused to speak to the issue at a news conference prior to the official opening of the assembly Sunday afternoon.
"All of us in America want to see Peru resolve these problems in a way that helps it strengthen democracy," he said, adding that "not only Peru" had problems to resolve.
Often lambasted as a talking-shop with little real influence, the 49-year-old OAS is determined to use the Lima assembly to change its image.
"Things won't stay on paper in the new OAS," promised Beatriz Ramacciotti, ambassador to the OAS for Peru.
As well as old problems, the region's new vogues for regional trade accords and free-market reforms were also expected to figure high on the OAS' 75-point agenda.
The preliminary Lima Declaration also contained promises to limit resources spent on conventional arms in favour of anti- poverty measures and environmental conservation.
The Peruvian government, still reeling from the four-month Lima hostage crisis, staged a huge security operation to prevent leftist guerrillas from sabotaging the assembly.
Both the Maoist Shining Path and the smaller Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) were planning attacks in Lima around this time, according to anti-terrorist police sources.
The MRTA stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in December, holding 72 VIP hostages for 126 days before troops stormed the building, killed the rebels and freed all but one of the captives.

A hero of that hostage crisis, Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, was due to chair the OAS assembly. One of the most high-ranking of the MRTA's hostages, Tudela narrowly escaped the residence alive after he was shot twice and a grenade exploded at his side in the rescue operation.
Tudela returned to the Foreign Ministry last week; he still uses a wheelchair.
